title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models

paper.title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward–reverse consistency force that joint positive–negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART ( Diffusion Reinforcement with A ggregation-First R eward T ilting), which aggregates each prompt’s rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 × 12.02\times and 11.72 × 11.72\times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Visual diffusion and flow-matching models 1 1 1 We use “diffusion” as a general term. Our paper targets rectified-flow with linear data–noise interpolation [ Lipman et al., 2022 ] , which shares the core principles of diffusion. are typically trained to fit the data distribution by regressing noise or velocity targets rather than to optimize downstream criteria such as visual quality, motion quality, or human preference, making reward-guided fine-tuning central to recent image and video generation tasks [ Xu et al., 2026a , Gao et al., 2025 ] . We focus on online diffusion Reinforcement Learning (RL), which, unlike differentiable reward-model optimization such as ReFL [ Xu et al., 2023 ] or offline preference learning such as Diffusion-DPO [ Wallace et al., 2023 ] , evaluates clean samples from the evolving generator and can use black-box rewards. Because these rewards arrive only after a complete output is generated, online diffusion RL faces a credit-assignment problem: costly output-level feedback must be translated into effective updates across many denoising states [ Liu et al., 2025a , Zheng et al., 2025 ] . Within this paradigm, reverse-process RL [ Black et al., 2023 ] , such as Flow-GRPO and its variants [ Liu et al., 2025a , Xue et al., 2025 , He et al., 2025 , Wang et al., 2026 ] , optimizes sampled denoising transitions via group-based endpoint reward feedback. It trains on states actually visited by the generator but requires ODE-to-SDE conversion for tractable likelihoods, and its policy gradient updates each selected transition along its own transition-level sampling noise, weighted by a trajectory-level advantage that this transition only partly determines, resulting in poor credit assignment and limiting training efficiency. Forward-process RL , such as DiffusionNFT [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] , instead applies forward noising to the generated clean samples and regresses velocities with reward-weighted positive and negative objectives. It needs no transition likelihoods and is highly efficient, but it is unstable without two stabilizers: joint positive–negative training and an exponential moving average (EMA) rollout policy whose lag must be tuned for each task [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] . Neither family is thus both efficient and stable without per-task tuning. In this paper, we focus on studying the instability of forward-process RL and developing a scalable algorithm which is both stable and efficient. We first examine NFT-style training, starting from a puzzle: its positive and negative branches share the same ideal reward-improving direction, so either alone should suffice, yet each alone collapses (Figure 2 (a)). We find that NFT’s targets, built from forward-noised endpoints, implicitly assume that the model’s sampling velocity equals the ideal forward velocity induced by its own endpoints. The two differ in practice, and the gap introduces a hidden non-reward-improving forward–reverse consistency force : the positive branch pulls each state’s velocity toward the ideal forward velocity and the negative branch pushes it away. Joint training can cancel this force but only partially, since reward centering balances rewards across samples rather than at each state. The residual can destabilize training and slow the reward optimization. We further show that EMA stabilizes NFT through the restoration force of its lagged reference, not through off-policy rollouts, but the EMA trick must be tuned per task. Driven by these insights, we introduce DiffusionART ( Diffusion Reinforcement with A ggregation-First R eward T ilting). It borrows supervised velocity regression from forward-process training but applies updates to states and actions during reverse-process rollouts. It first aggregates each prompt’s samples and rewards into a shared reward-improving direction G ⁡ ( c ) G(c) , then regresses each visited state’s action toward its guided target (Section 4.1 ). As this target never involves the forward velocity, the consistency force is removed by construction rather than by cross-sample cancellation, and each state receives an explicit reward-improving direction instead of a scalar advantage passed through likelihood ratios. A second update with a trust-region mask mechanism on each rollout adds a restoration force proportional to each state’s drift, replacing EMA with no schedule to tune (Section 4.2 ). We summarize our main contributions as follows: Main Contributions 1. Diagnosing the instability of NFT-style training. The NFT objective implicitly contains a harmful forward–reverse consistency force that joint training cancels only partially (Section 3.1 ). 2. Identifying restoration as the key stabilizer. EMA stabilizes NFT through restoration rather than off-policy data, but requires per-task tuning (Section 3.2 ). 3. Aggregation-first reward tilting with adaptive restoration. DiffusionART removes the consistency force by construction, eliminating the need for EMA with drift-adaptive restoration (Section 4 ). 4. Efficient and stable training. DiffusionART matches the strongest baseline’s efficiency on SD3.5-M without EMA or per-task tuning. Under VQ:MQ = 1 : 1 =1{:}1 weights on HunyuanVideo-13B, it reaches the late-stage mean VQ and MQ rewards of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 × 12.02\times and 11.72 × 11.72\times fewer GPU hours, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards, respectively. For image-to-video generation, it reaches MQ 6 with 4.8 × 4.8\times fewer GPU hours than Flow-GRPO-Fast (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 3 Understanding NFT-style Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: DiffusionNFT is highly efficient, but its stability relies on joint positive–negative training and an off-policy EMA rollout policy [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] . We examine why both are needed and where they fall short: joint training only partially cancels a hidden forward–reverse consistency force, while EMA provides restoration whose strength requires task-specific tuning. These limitations motivate the two components of DiffusionART in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Off-Policy EMA: Stability through Restoration, at the Cost of Task-Specific Tuning
sections.text: Figure 3: (a) On-policy DiffusionNFT without EMA ( β = 1 \beta=1 ): increasing number of micro-batches per rollout from 1 to 2 results in 15.2 × 15.2\times slower training. The dashed curve is the one-update run’s gradient norm, spiking as the reward collapses. (b) EMA-policy rollouts without the old-policy anchor still collapse. (c) At the second update, averaged over rollouts 0–17, restoration has a 9.4 × 9.4\times smaller output-force RMS but a 4.9 × 4.9\times larger parameter-gradient norm than guidance. Why EMA is not enough. EMA controls restoration indirectly through the reference policy’s lag: too little restoration risks collapse, while too much slows reward improvement. Its schedule therefore requires task-specific tuning. This suggests that heterogeneous per-sample guidance largely cancels across states, while restoration survives aggregation and dominates the update, slowing reward optimization. We leave a detailed analysis to our future work. sections.heading: 4 DiffusionART: Aggregation-first Reward Tilting with Adaptive Restoration
sections.text: DiffusionART (Algorithm 1 ) combines the advantages of forward- and reverse-process RL, while avoiding their limitations. It applies aggregation-first reward guidance to reverse-rollout states (section 4.1 ) and uses a second MSE update for drift-adaptive restoration (section 4.2 ), addressing the two failure modes identified in Section 3. A trust-region mechanism for an ODE solver further avoids excessive policy updates (section 4.3 ).

sections.heading: 4.4 Extension to Pairwise Reward Models
sections.text: Unlike math or code, visual outputs often lack objectively verifiable correctness criteria, making pairwise preferences a natural alternative to scalar scores for reward modeling [ Kirstain et al., 2023 ] . DiffusionART-Pairwise is a variant of DiffusionART which naturally supports online pairwise preference feedback [ Kirstain et al., 2023 ] . For each prompt, we divide K K endpoints into K / 2 K/2 disjoint pairs and assign winner/loser labels ( 1 , 0 ) (1,0) , or ( 1 / 2 , 1 / 2 ) (1/2,1/2) for ties. These labels replace scalar rewards in the otherwise unchanged covariance and training pipeline. Appendix C.3 provides the covariance formulation and pseudocode.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We study the efficiency, stability, and scalability of DiffusionART, progressing from text-to-image (T2I) generation to larger models and higher-dimensional text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V) generation.

sections.heading: 5.1 Text-to-Image Generation
sections.text: Setup. We compare DiffusionART with Flow-GRPO, Flow-GRPO-Fast (CPS) [ Liu et al., 2025a , Wang and Yu, 2025 ] , DanceGRPO [ Xue et al., 2025 ] , Flow-DPPO [ Ping et al., 2026 ] , and DiffusionNFT [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] with and without EMA, denoted DiffusionNFT (EMA) and DiffusionNFT (on-policy). All methods train LoRA adapters [ Hu et al., 2021 ] with rank r = 32 r=32 and scaling factor α = 64 \alpha=64 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, without CFG or reference-policy KL regularization. On SD3.5-M, we use a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and 10-step rollouts. DiffusionNFT uses the original per-task hyperparameters [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] to maximize its baseline performance. Single- and multi-reward optimization. We evaluate SD3.5-M [ Stability AI, 2024 ] on GenEval [ Ghosh et al., 2023 ] , OCR, and PickScore [ Kirstain et al., 2023 ] , and further jointly optimize GenEval, PickScore, CLIPScore [ Hessel et al., 2021 ] , and HPSv2.1 [ Wu et al., 2023 ] . Figure 5 (a–d) shows that DiffusionART behaves similarly under single- and multi-reward training. Figure 5 (d) plots the total reward, with components in Appendix A.4 . Without per-task EMA tuning, DiffusionART avoids the severe collapse of DiffusionNFT (on-policy) and achieves training efficiency comparable to DiffusionNFT (EMA). It is also much faster than Flow-GRPO, reaching Flow-GRPO’s step-500 reward with 10.0 × 10.0\times , 5.2 × 5.2\times , and 9.6 × 9.6\times fewer training steps on GenEval, OCR, and PickScore, respectively. Figure 5: Training rewards: (a–c) single- and (d) multi-reward SD3.5-M. Scaling to larger models. We extend the same recipe to FLUX.1-dev (12B) [ Black Forest Labs, 2024 ] on GenEval, using six-step rollouts and its built-in guidance embedding at scale 3.5, without additional CFG. For DiffusionNFT, we retain β = 1 \beta=1 and rollout-policy EMA decay min ⁡ ( 0.001 ​ n , 0.5 ) \min(0.001n,0.5) from the SD3.5-M GenEval baseline, where n n counts successful training updates. As shown in Figure 6 (a), DiffusionART learns fastest among all methods, while DiffusionNFT exhibits pronounced training-reward fluctuations because these hyperparameters are not retuned for FLUX. Table 2 in Appendix A.1 reports the GenEval evaluation scores of different methods at step 500. Figure 6: (a) FLUX.1-dev on GenEval. (b) Guidance and restoration ablation on OCR. Ablation of guidance and restoration. Figure 6 (b) compares ART: 1 update and ART: 2 updates , two DiffusionART variants with the same covariance guidance, against NFT: 2 updates with a carefully tuned β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 . As explained in Appendix B.3 , ART: 1 update learns quickly but gradually deteriorates. The second update in ART: 2 updates introduces restoration and provides long-term stability. sections.text: Setup. We fine-tune all parameters of the CFG-distilled HunyuanVideo-13B model [ Kong et al., 2024 ] with a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} and no KL regularization. Each group-based rollout uses 32 prompts and 8 videos per prompt. We generate 53-frame videos at 480 × 480 480\times 480 and 8 FPS with 16 sampling steps. VideoReward [ Liu et al., 2025b ] scores videos at 4 FPS for training and evaluation. All methods use matched TA:VQ:MQ weights of 7 : 2 : 1 7{:}2{:}1 to improve output quality while preserving prompt following. Figure 7 (a–c) compares all three rewards over 400 training steps; Appendix A.5 reports an additional VQ:MQ = 1 : 1 =1{:}1 comparison. Performance. As shown in Figure 7 , DiffusionART surpasses all baselines in both VQ and MQ while keeping TA comparable with the strongest baseline. DiffusionART reaches training VQ of 6 and MQ of 3 after 29 and 46 steps, respectively; Flow-GRPO-Fast, DanceGRPO, and DiffusionNFT (EMA) do not reach these levels within their recorded trajectories. For VQ of 5.5, DiffusionART needs 24 steps and 63.4 GPU hours, versus 273 steps and 1,401.4 GPU hours for DiffusionNFT (EMA): 11.4 × \times fewer training steps and 22.1 × \times fewer GPU hours . It retains its gains through 400 steps and achieves evaluation VQ and MQ of 8.970 and 4.224, as reported in Table 3 . DiffusionART improves evaluation VQ and MQ by 31.4% and 57.4%, respectively, over the strongest baseline. Figure 7: Efficient reward improvement across video generation. sections.heading: 5.3 Image-to-Video Generation
sections.text: Setup. We fine-tune all parameters of the CFG- and step-distilled Wan2.1-I2V-14B model [ Wan Team, 2025 ] released by LightX2V [ LightX2V, 2025 ] . Each rollout uses 32 prompts, FLUX.1-dev reference images, and 8 videos per prompt. We generate 53-frame videos at 400 × 640 400\times 640 and 8 FPS with four sampling steps. All methods use VQ:MQ = 1 : 1 =1{:}1 weights, a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and no KL regularization. Reward-model settings follow Section 5.2 . Performance. DiffusionART improves both VQ and MQ efficiently, whereas the baselines improve slowly or plateau (Figure 7 (d–e)). It reaches MQ of 6 in 45.8 GPU hours versus 220.3 for Flow-GRPO-Fast, a 4.8 × \times reduction . DiffusionNFT plateaus early and remains near that plateau through 400 updates, which we attribute to the residual self-consistency force diluting reward-improving guidance after gradient aggregation. Evaluation results are in Table 4 .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied why NFT-style forward-process diffusion post-training can be unstable and found that its objective can introduce an implicit forward–reverse self-consistency force that is not reliably canceled across states, while stronger restoration can improve stability at the cost of slower reward optimization. DiffusionART presents a simple but effective way to systematically cancel the unstable force by aggregating endpoint reward guidance before assigning it to reverse-rollout states, and then using a second update with a trust-region mechanism to provide drift-adaptive restoration for stabilization. Experiments on image and video generation show efficient, stable reward improvement, including with pairwise feedback and small rollout groups. Beyond the algorithm, our work provides insights into forward-process training, offering a clearer understanding of diffusion reinforcement learning and a path toward scalable diffusion post-training for visual generation.

It uses 44.2 GPU hours, versus 250.2 and 502.5, giving 5.7 × \times and 11.4 × \times GPU-hour speedups . DanceGRPO reaches this level after 821 steps and 1805.5 GPU hours. sections.heading: A.7 Trust-Region Masking Diagnostics
sections.text: We further inspect the matched HunyuanVideo comparison with VQ:MQ weights of 1 : 1 1{:}1 . Without masking, training exhibits larger late-stage gradient and velocity-drift spikes (Figure 13 ), complementing the reward curves in Figure 8 (a–b). Over the shared first 300 training steps, the maximum first-update gradient norm is 1.96 with masking, compared with 3.33 without it. The velocity drift measured before second updates, which reflects displacement caused by the first update, also shows much larger spikes without masking (Figure 13 ). Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.12572v1 [cs.LG] 08 Oct 2026 DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models Zhenglin Wan 1,2 Jiayu Chen 2,† Zhengfeiyang Zhang 1 Pengfei Zhou 1 Wangbo Zhao 3 Fangyuan Kong 2 Pengfei Wan 2 Kun Gai 2 Yang You 1 1 HPC-AI Lab, National University of Singapore 2 Kling AI 3 HKUST Email: vanzl@u.nus.edu , jia768167535@gmail.com GitHub: https://github.com/vanzll/DiffusionART Project Page: https://vanzll.github.io/diffusionart-project/ Abstract Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward–reverse consistency force that joint positive–negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART ( Diffusion Reinforcement with A ggregation-First R eward T ilting), which aggregates each prompt’s rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 × 12.02\times and 11.72 × 11.72\times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding author. Figure 1: Efficient learning and improved generations. Left: Mean of raw VQ and MQ (equal weights). Right: Selected same-prompt images and video frames before and after DiffusionART. 1 Introduction Visual diffusion and flow-matching models 1 1 1 We use “diffusion” as a general term. Our paper targets rectified-flow with linear data–noise interpolation [ Lipman et al., 2022 ] , which shares the core principles of diffusion. are typically trained to fit the data distribution by regressing noise or velocity targets rather than to optimize downstream criteria such as visual quality, motion quality, or human preference, making reward-guided fine-tuning central to recent image and video generation tasks [ Xu et al., 2026a , Gao et al., 2025 ] . We focus on online diffusion Reinforcement Learning (RL), which, unlike differentiable reward-model optimization such as ReFL [ Xu et al., 2023 ] or offline preference learning such as Diffusion-DPO [ Wallace et al., 2023 ] , evaluates clean samples from the evolving generator and can use black-box rewards. Because these rewards arrive only after a complete output is generated, online diffusion RL faces a credit-assignment problem: costly output-level feedback must be translated into effective updates across many denoising states [ Liu et al., 2025a , Zheng et al., 2025 ] . Within this paradigm, reverse-process RL [ Black et al., 2023 ] , such as Flow-GRPO and its variants [ Liu et al., 2025a , Xue et al., 2025 , He et al., 2025 , Wang et al., 2026 ] , optimizes sampled denoising transitions via group-based endpoint reward feedback. It trains on states actually visited by the generator but requires ODE-to-SDE conversion for tractable likelihoods, and its policy gradient updates each selected transition along its own transition-level sampling noise, weighted by a trajectory-level advantage that this transition only partly determines, resulting in poor credit assignment and limiting training efficiency. Forward-process RL , such as DiffusionNFT [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] , instead applies forward noising to the generated clean samples and regresses velocities with reward-weighted positive and negative objectives. It needs no transition likelihoods and is highly efficient, but it is unstable without two stabilizers: joint positive–negative training and an exponential moving average (EMA) rollout policy whose lag must be tuned for each task [ Zheng et al., 2025 ] . Neither family is thus both efficient and stable without per-task tuning. In this paper, we focus on studying the instability of forward-process RL and developing a scalable algorithm which is both stable and efficient. We first examine NFT-style training, starting from a puzzle: its positive and negative branches share the same ideal reward-improving direction, so either alone should suffice, yet each alone collapses (Figure 2 (a)). We find that NFT’s targets, built from forward-noised endpoints, implicitly assume that the model’s sampling velocity equals the ideal forward velocity induced by its own endpoints. The two differ in practice, and the gap introduces a hidden non-reward-improving forward–reverse consistency force : the positive branch pulls each state’s velocity toward the ideal forward velocity and the negative branch pushes it away. Joint training can cancel this force but only partially, since reward centering balances rewards across samples rather than at each state. The residual can destabilize training and slow the reward optimization. We further show that EMA stabilizes NFT through the restoration force of its lagged reference, not through off-policy rollouts, but the EMA trick must be tuned per task. Driven by these insights, we introduce DiffusionART ( Diffusion Reinforcement with A ggregation-First R eward T ilting). It borrows supervised velocity regression from forward-process training but applies updates to states and actions during reverse-process rollouts. It first aggregates each prompt’s samples and rewards into a shared reward-improving direction G ⁡ ( c ) G(c) , then regresses each visited state’s action toward its guided target (Section 4.1 ). As this target never involves the forward velocity, the consistency force is removed by construction rather than by cross-sample cancellation, and each state receives an explicit reward-improving direction instead of a scalar advantage passed through likelihood ratios. A second update with a trust-region mask mechanism on each rollout adds a restoration force proportional to each state’s drift, replacing EMA with no schedule to tune (Section 4.2 ). We summarize our main contributions as follows: Main Contributions 1. Diagnosing the instability of NFT-style training. The NFT objective implicitly contains a harmful forward–reverse consistency force that joint training cancels only partially (Section 3.1 ). 2. Identifying restoration as the key stabilizer. EMA stabilizes NFT through restoration rather than off-policy data, but requires per-task tuning (Section 3.2 ). 3. Aggregation-first reward tilting with adaptive restoration. DiffusionART removes the consistency force by construction, eliminating the need for EMA with drift-adaptive restoration (Section 4 ). 4. Efficient and stable training. DiffusionART matches the strongest baseline’s efficiency on SD3.5-M without EMA or per-task tuning. Under VQ:MQ = 1 : 1 =1{:}1 weights on HunyuanVideo-13B, it reaches the late-stage mean VQ and MQ rewards of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 × 12.02\times and 11.72 × 11.72\times fewer GPU hours, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards, respectively. Evaluation results are in Table 4 . 6 Conclusion We studied why NFT-style forward-process diffusion post-training can be unstable and found that its objective can introduce an implicit forward–reverse self-consistency force that is not reliably canceled across states, while stronger restoration can improve stability at the cost of slower reward optimization. DiffusionART presents a simple but effective way to systematically cancel the unstable force by aggregating endpoint reward guidance before assigning it to reverse-rollout states, and then using a second update with a trust-region mechanism to provide drift-adaptive restoration for stabilization. Experiments on image and video generation show efficient, stable reward improvement, including with pairwise feedback and small rollout groups. Beyond the algorithm, our work provides insights into forward-process training, offering a clearer understanding of diffusion reinforcement learning and a path toward scalable diffusion post-training for visual generation. 7 Acknowledgement We thank Kaiwen Zheng and Huayu Chen for the insightful discussion about the intuition behind DiffusionNFT and the valuable suggestion for the experiment design.
